messages.subject: Re: AKDE and cyclical fix schedule
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I realised the fitted.mods is just a container that I created for the outputs of ctmm.select(). Sorry for the confusion!

After calculating the uere from my calibration data, I have a couple of simple questions about the uere and how it is applied. I read through the pre-print  <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v1.full>you suggested, but just thought it best to clarify with you:

1. How is the uere used to transform the hdop to a location error in metres? Is the hdop multiplied by the uere for a each point?
2. Are the values provided from summary(uere) in metres?
3. Is it unusual for the 2D fixes to have a better 'accuracy' compared to 3D fixes, or could this be the result of a skew in the number of 2D and 3D fixes in the calibration data set?
(I used a calibration dataset of 642 points from 6 of the same model of GPS data logger, 13 points were 2D and 615 were 3D. Collected over the period of a week)

          low             est               high
3D    6.128738   6.382168   6.635461
2D    3.808311   5.220041   6.629224

Cheers,
Cass

On Wednesday, November 25, 2020 at 11:40:10 PM UTC+10 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Cass,
>
> I don't recognize fitted.mods() either. Maybe you have a script from someone?
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Wednesday, November 25, 2020 at 12:37:14 AM UTC-5 cassandra....@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi Chris,
> >
> > Not a problem re  CI="Gauss", I'll leave that out and instead try to model the error and calibrate my tracking data as you suggest.
> >
> > Apologies, I meant fitted.mods function in ctmm.
> >
> > Thanks for the information on windowed analysis. I think this is also likely to be relevant to bilbies as they commonly shift around their network of burrows, particularly after females have weaned young. I look forward to seeing how ctmm develops over time to incorporate these types of shifts, as it's a great package to use.
> >
> > Thanks for your assistance with this, I appreciate it.
> >
> > Kind regards,
> > Cass.
> > On Wednesday, November 25, 2020 at 2:41:09 AM UTC+10 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hi Cass,
> > >
> > > CI="Gauss" requires better data quality than the default setting (because it has to reference the semi-variance at smaller lags to estimate the CIs at larger lags) and it looks like it isn't going to be able to cooperate with the gaps in your data. I would go back to what you were doing. Sorry about that.
> > >
> > > I'm not familiar with fitted.models(). What package is that from? I would go with the selected model, though those look pretty similar.
> > >
> > > Those model fits look to be a little bit above the empirical variograms, though not as much as the end of the first plot you shared. That could be from a mild amount of range shifting or it could be bias from the location error not being modeled yet.
> > >
> > > The first thing I would do is to model the error and calibrate your tracking data. If you calculate your variogram from calibrated data with fast=FALSE, then that also improves the quality of the variogram (for data with relatively large location errors). Your 1-day ranges appear to be ~5-10 hectares (200-300 meters)^2, and GPS location errors tend to be 10-100 meters, and possibly more of the latter with a burrowing species. Given that those scales are similar, you can get substantial bias in both the empirical variograms and the fitted models, if you don't model the error.
> > >
> > > If you still see the discrepancy, then I would consider trying to either segment the data (if that appears possible), which is more for animals that shift their range suddenly, or doing a windowed analysis if the range shifting is more continuous. Armadillos tend to move around a network of burrows and often need the latter. In the future, we will have more complex models that can incorporate random range shifts like.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris
> > >
> > > On Monday, November 23, 2020 at 8:33:44 PM UTC-5 cassandra....@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hi Chris,
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for replying so promptly.
> > > >
> > > > I will read through the article you suggest for selecting an error model and try that with my data. It is also good to know that I don't need to apply the weights, I did notice that it included some additional burrows within the HR plots compared to non-weighted AKDE.
> > > >
> > > > Following your suggestion, I included CI="Gauss" in the calculation of the variogram. I then used variogram.fit() and manually selected starting values for the model parameters that were a close fit to the first couple of weeks of data. I then fitted and compared the various models with fitted.models(). From looking at the plots, none of the "top 3" models appear to be a good fit to me (attached). But they also seem to have clipped the data period down to that 15 day period.
> > > >
> > > > A couple of questions:
> > > >
> > > > 1. Is there a reason it would be clipped to just the first 15 days for these plots?
> > > > 2. Should I continue to trial other starting values, or do you think this is a case of needing to segment my data as you mentioned in your reply?
> > > >
> > > > I will also have a look at the data for other bilbies and see if this variation is common.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again,
> > > > Cass
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, November 24, 2020 at 4:54:17 AM UTC+10 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > Hi Cass,
> > > > >
> > > > > Rather than applying an HDOP threshold, I would recommend taking your stationary testing data and using that to select an error model and calibrating your tracking data: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v1
> > > > > At scales this small, a good error model could potentially have some impact on your estimates.
> > > > >
> > > > > 1. If these are nocturnal data and you are only sampling at night, then you don't need to apply AKDE weights. In fact, if your data starts and ends at the burrows, then the weights are going to bias towards the burrows, because the model doesn't know that the start/end times are any different from the midnight times.
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. The first ~half month of that variogram looks great for home-range estimation. The gap isn't an issue. Continuous-time models can handle gaping, even if it makes the variograms ugly (though the dt argument can help with that, as in the vignette example). What is potentially concerning is the possible increase in variance at the end. If that's real, then I would be concerned as to whether or not your bilby had a range shift. CI="Gauss" can improve the confidence interval calculation, but the better test is whether or not the selected model hugs the initial asymptote or is higher (like at the end of the variogram), in which case I would try to segment your data. I have heard good things about segclust2d for that.
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Chris
> > > > >
> > > > > On Monday, November 23, 2020 at 3:11:47 AM UTC-5 cassandra....@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have been working my way through the vignettes to estimate home ranges of bilbies I have GPS tracking data for (nocturnal, burrowing marsupials).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As they are only active at night, I have scheduled fixes to be collected hourly from dusk til dawn to maximise the battery life of the units. There are also some gaps in the data due to a range of factors (ie GPS failure, different data collection periods etc).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Prior to importing my data, I cleaned out any outliers, invalid fixes and fixes that exceeded a set HDOP threshold as determined through stationary testing of the units.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have a couple of questions about how to best process my data that I am hoping you can help me with:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 1. As I have missing/irregular data, I have been comparing different models including a weighted AKDE model (using function weights=TRUE). Is this enough to account for the cyclical nature of the GPS fixes and the gaps in data, or should I also consider other functions?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2. Does the variogram below look suitable for a home range analysis in ctmm? I note there is a large gap and then an increase in variation, though the scale of the variation appears quite small.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I was really impressed at how easy it was to learn the basic workflows for ctmm from the paper in Methods in Ecology and Evolution - a great paper, thank you!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks in advance.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Kind regards,
> > > > > > Cass
> > > > > >
> > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: AKDE and cyclical fix schedule
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cass,

1. Yes, with some factors of sqrt(2) and whatnot.
2. Yes, and I will update the documentation to reflect that.
3. In this case, the confidence intervals of the rarely sampled 2D fixes are wide enough that I doubt model selection will support there being two location classes. I would merge them by deleting the class column before or after import. You can then check how this impacts AIC/BIC and the goodness-of-fit statistic. I doubt there will be support for 2D and 3D fixes having different parameters.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for building the meta() function so that the above is now easy! I had a related question - I would like to analyze differences in estimated home range overlap across categories - the overlap() outputs are an array with the estimate and the CI, how can I get variance or standard error to use in a meta-analysis with the metafor package?

Thank you!

Rachel

> > 2) calculate SE from the CI
> >

> > Jared

messages.subject: Re: SE / Var for model estimate of HR
messages.subject_clean: SE / Var for model estimate of HR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

I'll put exposing that on the TODO list, but for the moment you could divide the CI width by a z-score CI width (2*1.96 @ 95%) to get an approximate standard error.

This won't account for the correlations between overlaps if you have a bunch of individuals in the same area. That's a whole 'nother paper.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: SE / Var for model estimate of HR
messages.subject_clean: SE / Var for model estimate of HR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

This is what you would want for the variance and standard error of the area (2D chi^2 relation):

S <- summary(UD)
AREA <- S$CI[1,2]
VAR <- AREA^2 / S$DOF['area']
SE <- sqrt(VAR)

And I would recommend something like a log-link, if possible, in which case you would actually want

log.AREA <- log(AREA)
VAR.log <- 1/ S$DOF['area']
SE.log <- sqrt(VAR.log)

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
messages.subject_clean: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

This thread is a bit old but would be curious to get some precision on one of your previous comment (July 1st 2020).

For summarizing the original background: I am working on a central-place foraging species, which under chick-rearing comes back and forth to its colony, roughly every ~ 4 hours. While computing individual-level home range estimates (via AKDE), I wanted to minimize the "colony weight" in order to focus on the "foraging behavior", meaning focusing only on locations outside the colony.

For doing so, I have removed all colony locations, except the first and the last points of each (complete) trip. Within trips, all locations are separated by a standard interval of 10 minutes. Since each individual has many trips (~ 4 trips/individual), I reshaped the timespan of each individual tracking period, having thus a 10 minutes interval between every individual's trip, resulting in a maximum time spent at the colony of 10 minutes. This approach was firstly intended to avoid large time gaps (~ 4-6 hours) between trips. By doing so, however, I was also changing the natural timespan of the tracking period, which ultimately was also affecting the estimates from the autocorrelation function.

On this approach, you stated previously:

ctmm is currently limited to stationary processes (with the simple exception of non-stationary mean functions), and that will be a longer-term upgrade. So it is a good idea to segment the data into individual behaviors before fitting a stationary model. If I understand what you are doing correctly, there does not need to be a maximum threshold of time between trips. You just want to have the nesting behavior removed.

By reading your comment again, I am now considering changing my approach: by simply removing all colony points (thus focusing on points outside the colony) while keeping the natural timespan between all locations. Doing so, however, will generate gaps of many hours during the tracking period (equivalent to the time spent at the colony). But as read in your paper (2018, Ecological Applications 28), the AKDE could deal with such missing locations.

My question: Would you recommend to consider using the original timespan of the tracking period while removing the locations from the colony, despite the imposed cyclical gaps in GPS location?

Hopefully, this thread could help other users dealing with CPF-based data. Thank you again for your ongoing help. /Phil

Since the overlap() function doesn't appear to be reliable when implemented with the average distributions (e.g. from mean.UD), I am searching for the most optimal way of aggregating data within the individual stratum. So far, I am considering continuous time between each individual's trip, and by removing the "extra" localisation at the colony (i.e. except the departure and arrival points to the colony). In other words, we have a regular interval of 10 min between every two locations within individuals, having thus a maximum of 10 min at the colony before the next trip.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

Yes, I don't think you need a maximum threshold of time between trips because the start and end points are both at the nest. In a completely different situation where you have segmented behaviors and those points are far apart, then you might want to dilate the time between to prevent long-ranged correlation.

If you plan to turn weights on in AKDE, then I would actually reduce the time between trips to the sampling interval, to avoid placing large weights on the colonies. But I would only worry about weights if the foraging period suffers irregular sampling.

Best,
Chris
